tldr: Nvidia's first quarter without Jensen Huang: revenue up 103% to $115.8 billion, and the board says he is not coming back.
US jets struck a Revolutionary Guard missile site on Qeshm Island; Bahrain and Kuwait intercepted Iranian munitions on Wednesday.
Traders have now fully priced a December Federal Reserve rate hike, with the 10-year Treasury yield above 5.1%.
A leukemia vaccine extended median survival to 24.0 months from 14.7 in its pivotal Phase 3 trial.
Anthropic prices the largest IPO on record tonight at $70 to $78 a share, valuing it near $1.4 trillion.
Xi met Trump personally at the Shenzhen airport, a day before the first three-way summit with Putin.
Britain sanctioned eight Israeli construction firms over West Bank settlements, freezing their assets.
The FDA approved Cosentyx for polymyalgia rheumatica, the first anti-IL-17 biologic cleared for the condition.
The FAA halted router installations nationwide after one new unit in Arkansas triggered a five-hour ground stop.
A judge ordered Trump to sit for a deposition in his own $10 billion suit against the BBC: “It is Trump's case.”

items.headline: Nvidia's revenue doubled in its first quarter without Jensen Huang
items.body: Nvidia reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, with data-center revenue of $107.6 billion, up 110%, and GAAP earnings of $2.70 a diluted share. It guided to $130 billion for the current quarter, above the $125.1 billion consensus, while assuming no data-center compute revenue from China at all. It was the first report since Jensen Huang resigned on November 12, and the board said separately that it does not intend to reinstate him.
items.plain: Nvidia designs the chips that almost all modern AI systems are trained and run on, so its sales are the clearest measure of how much companies are really spending on AI. Sales doubled in a year. The striking part is the forecast: Nvidia expects $130 billion next quarter while assuming it sells no AI computing power into China at all. It is growing this fast with what was once its second-largest market written down to zero.
items.why: Nvidia's order book is the one number that can confirm or deny the AI capital-spending boom, and it just said demand is strong enough that losing China entirely does not slow it down.

items.headline: US and Iran trade strikes around the Strait of Hormuz, and Gulf states intercept the overflow
items.body: US fighter jets struck a Revolutionary Guard missile launch site on Iran's Qeshm Island on Tuesday, hours after Iranian drones targeted a US radar at Bahrain's Sheikh Isa Air Base. Bahrain said it intercepted “a number of Iranian aerial attacks” early Wednesday and Kuwait reported interceptions too, while a tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, with 21 Indian nationals evacuated, two injured and one missing. Iran's deputy governor of Hormozgan province said the Qeshm strike damaged no vital infrastructure; US officials called it self-defense.
items.plain: Qeshm is an Iranian island at the mouth of the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea passage that roughly a fifth of the world's oil travels through. That geography is the point: missiles on Qeshm can reach the shipping lane, and the lane is Iran's main leverage. The pattern now is exchange rather than escalation, each side hitting a military target and calling it defensive. The civilian cost is landing on commercial ships and their crews.
items.why: Every round makes direct strikes between the United States and Iran more routine, and shipping and insurance markets price that in long before diplomats acknowledge it.

items.headline: Markets have fully priced a December rate hike, six weeks after the Fed held steady
items.body: Traders put roughly a 95% chance on the Federal Reserve raising rates a quarter point at its December 9 meeting, according to CME's FedWatch tool, with the prediction market Kalshi pricing a hike of any size at 97%. October retail sales rose 0.2% on the month, in line with forecasts, while sales excluding gas and autos came in stronger than expected; the 10-year Treasury yield sat near 5.11%. Governor Christopher Waller has said a half-point move should be considered in December because October core CPI came in at 0.3%, his stated threshold.
items.plain: The Federal Reserve raises interest rates to slow spending when prices climb too fast, making borrowing more expensive for everyone from homebuyers to corporations. It held rates steady in October, so a December hike would be a reversal, not a continuation. What flipped the odds was inflation: consumer prices rose 0.4% in one month, and wholesale prices are up 6.5% over the year. Shoppers are still spending, which removes the Fed's reason to wait.
items.why: Pricing this certain, this quickly, means the argument inside the Fed has moved from how fast to cut to how hard to tighten.

items.headline: A leukemia vaccine added nine months of median survival in a Phase 3 trial
items.body: SELLAS Life Sciences said its Phase 3 REGAL trial of galinpepimut-S, a therapeutic cancer vaccine, met its primary endpoint in acute myeloid leukemia, with median overall survival of 24.0 months against 14.7 months for best available treatment. That is a hazard ratio of 0.59, a 41% reduction in the risk of death, with a two-sided p-value of 0.035 across 126 randomized patients, all ineligible for a transplant and in a second or later remission. These are topline figures from the company; no full dataset has been published and the FDA has not reviewed them.
items.plain: Acute myeloid leukemia is a fast-moving cancer of the blood and bone marrow. This is a therapeutic vaccine: it does not prevent an infection but trains the immune system to recognize a protein leukemia cells overproduce, so the body attacks the cancer if it returns. Patients lived about nine months longer. Two cautions: the trial is small at 126 patients and covers only people whose cancer already came back, and the numbers come from the company, not a peer-reviewed paper.
items.why: Therapeutic cancer vaccines have failed in late-stage trials for two decades, so a clean randomized survival result revives an entire class of treatment that most of the field had written off.

items.headline: Anthropic prices the largest IPO on record tonight, at a valuation marked down from September
items.body: Anthropic set a price range of $70 to $78 a share for 825 million shares, is expected to price the offering on the evening of November 18, and begins trading on Nasdaq as ANT on November 19. The top of the range implies a fully diluted valuation near $1.4 trillion and a raise of about $61 billion at the midpoint, with Bloomberg reporting orders at nearly seven times the shares available. That is well below the roughly $2 trillion the company targeted as recently as September.
items.plain: An IPO is the first time a private company sells shares to the general public. Anthropic builds Claude, a competitor to ChatGPT. Two numbers tell the story at once. The raise, around $61 billion, would be the largest ever, because training frontier AI models burns cash on a scale no earlier software company needed. Yet the valuation is down from about $2 trillion in September after AI stocks sold off. Demand is enormous and the price is a markdown, simultaneously.
items.why: It sets the first public market price for a frontier AI lab, and every other lab's next funding round will be measured against it.

items.headline: Xi met Trump at the airport in Shenzhen, a day before the first three-way summit with Putin
items.body: Trump landed in Shenzhen for the APEC summit and was met at the airport by Xi Jinping, an unusually personal greeting for a visiting leader, then greeted Vladimir Putin at the welcome banquet. The three hold the first trilateral meeting of its kind on Thursday, with nuclear arms reduction, Ukraine and Iran on the agenda. A senior US official called the session an “entry point” and said no agreement is anticipated, while China's foreign ministry has said it would be “neither fair, reasonable nor realistic” to ask China to join trilateral disarmament negotiations at this stage.
items.plain: APEC is an annual economic summit of countries around the Pacific, and the real business happens in side meetings. The US and Russia hold the large majority of the world's nuclear warheads; China's arsenal is far smaller but growing, which is why Beijing objects to being seated as an equal third. A three-way arms control conversation has never happened before. Both the American official and the Chinese statement point the same way: expect a photograph, not a treaty.
items.why: Pulling China into what has always been a US-Russia arms control framework is the central American arms control goal of the decade, and Beijing has now said in public that it will not play.

items.headline: Britain sanctions eight Israeli construction firms over West Bank settlements
items.body: Britain sanctioned eight Israeli construction and property companies involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, along with an activist group that has blocked aid deliveries to Gaza. The measures freeze assets and bar those named from forming or managing companies in the UK, and they land ahead of final tender deadlines for the E1 settlement project. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the move a “hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies” and said Israel would respond; the Palestinian Authority's foreign ministry welcomed it.
items.plain: The West Bank is Palestinian territory Israel has occupied since 1967, where it has built housing for Israeli citizens that most of the world considers illegal under international law. Britain is not sanctioning the Israeli government here, it is going after the builders and their money, which is a different lever: a firm cut off from British banks and company registration has a harder time financing construction. E1 is a large planned settlement east of Jerusalem that critics say would split the West Bank in two.
items.why: Sanctioning the contractors rather than the state is a lever other European governments can copy without a formal diplomatic break with Israel.

items.headline: FDA approves Cosentyx for polymyalgia rheumatica, the first anti-IL-17 biologic for the disease
items.body: The FDA approved Novartis's Cosentyx, or secukinumab, at 150 mg for adults with polymyalgia rheumatica whose response to corticosteroids is inadequate or who cannot tolerate a steroid taper, making it the first anti-IL-17 biologic cleared for the condition and the drug's 11th US indication. Approval rests on the Phase 3 REPLENISH trial, in which 40.5% of patients on Cosentyx reached sustained remission at week 52 against 20.5% on placebo, across 27 countries, with both arms following a 24-week steroid taper. One secukinumab-treated patient died of cryptococcal meningitis.
items.plain: Polymyalgia rheumatica causes severe pain and stiffness in the shoulders and hips, mostly in people over 50. The standard treatment is steroids, which work but cause bone loss, diabetes and infections when taken for months or years, so the goal of any new drug is getting patients off them. Cosentyx blocks an immune signaling protein called IL-17. Twice as many patients stayed in remission, though that still means most on the drug did not.
items.why: Steroid-sparing is the real prize in inflammatory disease, and this gives older patients a documented route off a drug class whose long-term harms are well established.

items.headline: The FAA paused its router upgrades nationwide after one new box in Arkansas stopped US flights
items.body: The FAA said Tuesday it is pausing installation of new routers nationwide after a newly installed Juniper unit at a remote radio site in southern Arkansas appeared to overwhelm the systems feeding radar data to air traffic control, triggering a nearly five-hour national ground stop on Friday, November 13. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said contractor L3Harris Technologies had just installed the router as part of an upgrade; one count put cancellations at 12,462 flights. The agency says there is no sign of a cyberattack and the full cause remains unclear.
items.plain: Air traffic control depends on a network carrying radar and flight data between facilities, and routers are the boxes that direct that traffic. One new router at a rural Arkansas site, installed as part of a modernization project, apparently pushed more data onto the network than older equipment could absorb, so a single upgrade in one building halted flights nationwide. The uncomfortable detail is that this was routine maintenance, not an attack. The FAA's response is to stop the modernization.
items.why: The program meant to make air traffic control more reliable is what broke it, and the immediate remedy is to halt the upgrade, which leaves the aging equipment in place through the Thanksgiving travel peak.

items.headline: Judge orders Trump to be deposed in the lawsuit he brought himself: "It is Trump's case"
items.body: A federal judge ordered Trump to sit for a deposition by January 22 in the $10 billion defamation suit he filed against the BBC. “It is Trump's case, so he should expect to be deposed,” Judge Jeffrey Kuntz wrote in a four-page order dated November 17, which extends a December 11 deadline set by a magistrate judge and requires both sides to be trial-ready by May 3. The BBC accepted Trump's own offer of a window between January 11 and 22, and he faces up to seven hours of questioning by BBC lawyers, not in public. The suit alleges the BBC spliced together clips of his January 6, 2021 speech; the BBC has apologized for the edit as misleading while denying liability for defamation.
items.plain: A deposition is sworn questioning by the opposing side's lawyers before trial, and lying during one is a crime. Trump chose to file this lawsuit, and the rule in American courts is that whoever sues must answer questions about the claims they brought. His side sought delay on the grounds that he is the sitting president; the judge's answer was that it is his own case. The result of suing over an edit of his speech is seven hours under oath about it.
items.why: Unlike the cases brought against him, this one is his to drop, so the deposition is a cost he chose and can now avoid only by abandoning a $10 billion claim.
